proofs.proof_tex:
First fix any positive integer \(n\) and any \(R\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\). If the defining set for \(\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(R)\) is empty, then \(\textnormal{def:equal-square-comparator}\) assigns it the value \(-\infty\), and the inequality
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(R)\ge\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(R)
\]
holds in the extended order.

Suppose instead that the defining set is nonempty, and let \(k\) be any eligible positive divisor of \(n\). Put \(r=n/k\), so \(r\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), and define a paired profile with \(L=2r\) and
\[
a_\ell=b_\ell=k\qquad(\ell\in[L]).
\]
The block sizes are positive, and their two covering sums are
\[
\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}a_\ell=Lk=2rk=2n,
\qquad
\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}b_\ell=Lk=2rk=2n.
\]
By \(\textnormal{def:common-support}\), positivity of \(k\) permits division in the half-sum equations and gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(a,b)
&=\left\{z\in\{0,1\}^{2r}:k\sum_{\ell=1}^{2r}z_\ell=n,\ k\sum_{\ell=1}^{2r}z_\ell=n\right\}\\
&=\left\{z\in\{0,1\}^{2r}:\sum_{\ell=1}^{2r}z_\ell=r\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(\textnormal{def:support-size}\) yields
\[
h(a,b)=\binom{2r}{r}=\binom{2n/k}{n/k}\ge R,
\]
where the inequality is exactly the eligibility condition in \(\textnormal{def:equal-square-comparator}\). The positivity, covering, and support calculations verify every membership condition in \(\textnormal{def:profile-class}\), so this equal-square profile belongs to \(\mathcal A_{n,n}(R)\). By \(\textnormal{def:retention}\), its retention is
\[
F(a,b)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{2r}k^2=2rk^2=2nk.
\]
The maximizing definition \(\textnormal{def:frontier}\) now implies \(\Phi_{n,n}(R)\ge2nk\) for every eligible \(k\). The eligible set is finite because every positive divisor \(k\) of \(n\) satisfies \(1\le k\le n\). Taking its maximum, as specified by \(\textnormal{def:equal-square-comparator}\), proves
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(R)\ge\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(R).
\]
Together with the empty-set case, this establishes the all-resolution dominance without any large-margin restriction.

Now let \(R=4\) and \(n\ge3\). The proved lemma \(\textnormal{lem:r4-least-divisor-classification}\) gives the sharper identities
\[
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=\frac{2n^2}{\ell(n)},
\qquad
\Phi_{n,n}(4)=2(n-1)^2+2,
\]
as well as the exact gap and exact ratio. That lemma also proves \(\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)\le n^2\), the gap bound \((n-2)^2>0\), and the displayed ratio lower bound, with equality in every weak bound exactly when \(n\) is even. Finally, it proves convergence of the ratio to \(2\) along the even integers and the matching global lower-limit inequality. These two facts give
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}=2.
\]
Thus every assertion of the theorem follows; the same lemma additionally supplies the exact least-divisor classification and the prime-size formulas.

added_lemmas.statement:
For every integer \(n\ge3\), let
\[
\ell(n)=\min\{d\in\mathbb Z:d\ge2,\ d\mid n\}.
\]
The published equal-square subclass at \(R=4\) has
\[
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=\frac{2n^2}{\ell(n)},
\]
whereas the covering paired-rectangle frontier has
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)=2(n-1)^2+2.
\]
Hence the exact gap and ratio are
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
=2(n-1)^2+2-\frac{2n^2}{\ell(n)}
\]
and
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
=\ell(n)\left(1-\frac2n+\frac{2}{n^2}\right).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)\le n^2,
\quad
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)\ge(n-2)^2>0,
\quad
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
\ge2-\frac4n+\frac4{n^2},
\]
and equality in each weak inequality holds if and only if \(n\) is even. The ratio has limit inferior \(2\) as \(n\to\infty\), attained asymptotically along the even integers. If \(n\) is prime, then
\[
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=2n,
\qquad
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=2(n-1)(n-2),
\qquad
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}=n-2+\frac2n.
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix an integer \(n\ge3\). The set
\[
\{d\in\mathbb Z:d\ge2,\ d\mid n\}
\]
is nonempty because it contains \(n\), and it is finite because every one of its elements lies between \(2\) and \(n\). Thus its minimum \(\ell(n)\) is well defined.

Let \(k\) be a positive divisor of \(n\), and set \(r=n/k\). By \(\textnormal{def:equal-square-comparator}\), \(k\) is eligible at \(R=4\) exactly when
\[
\binom{2n/k}{n/k}=\binom{2r}{r}\ge4,
\]
and the corresponding retained focal count is \(2nk\). If \(k=n\), then \(r=1\) and
\[
\binom{2r}{r}=\binom21=2<4,
\]
so \(k=n\) is ineligible.

If \(k<n\), then the positive integer \(r=n/k\) satisfies \(r\ge2\). Direct calculation gives \(\binom42=6\). For every integer \(s\ge1\), all factorials below are positive, so division is valid and
\[
\frac{\binom{2(s+1)}{s+1}}{\binom{2s}{s}}
=\frac{(2s+2)(2s+1)}{(s+1)^2}
=\frac{2(2s+1)}{s+1}>1,
\]
because \(2(2s+1)-(s+1)=3s+1>0\). Induction from \(s=2\) yields
\[
\binom{2r}{r}\ge\binom42=6\ge4.
\]
Consequently, the eligible \(k\)'s are exactly the proper positive divisors of \(n\).

The score \(2nk\) is strictly increasing in \(k\), since \(2n>0\). The map \(k\mapsto d=n/k\) is a bijection from the proper positive divisors \(k\) of \(n\) to the divisors \(d\) of \(n\) satisfying \(d\ge2\), and the map \(d\mapsto n/d\) is order reversing on positive \(d\). Therefore the largest eligible block size is \(n/\ell(n)\). The set optimized in \(\textnormal{def:equal-square-comparator}\) is nonempty here (for example, \(k=1\) is a proper divisor), and hence
\[
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
=2n\frac{n}{\ell(n)}
=\frac{2n^2}{\ell(n)}.
\]
This value is strictly positive because \(n\ge3\) and \(2\le\ell(n)\le n\).

Applying the already established \(\textnormal{prop:r4-reduction}\) with \(n_B=n_S=n\ge3\) gives
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)=2(n-1)^2+2.
\]
Subtracting the equal-square value gives the exact gap
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
=2(n-1)^2+2-\frac{2n^2}{\ell(n)}.
\]
Because \(\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)>0\), division is legitimate, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
&=\frac{2(n-1)^2+2}{2n^2/\ell(n)}\\
&=\ell(n)\frac{(n-1)^2+1}{n^2}\\
&=\ell(n)\left(1-\frac2n+\frac{2}{n^2}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(\ell(n)\ge2\),
\[
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=\frac{2n^2}{\ell(n)}\le n^2.
\]
Substitution into the exact gap gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
&\ge2(n-1)^2+2-n^2\\
&=(n-2)^2>0,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the strict inequality follows from \(n\ge3\). Also
\[
1-\frac2n+\frac{2}{n^2}
=\frac{(n-1)^2+1}{n^2}>0,
\]
so multiplying \(\ell(n)\ge2\) by this positive factor gives
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
\ge2-\frac4n+\frac4{n^2}.
\]
Equality in any one of these three weak inequalities is equivalent to \(\ell(n)=2\). By the definition of \(\ell(n)\), this is equivalent to \(2\mid n\), hence to \(n\) being even.

The lower bound \(2-4/n+4/n^2\) tends to \(2\), so
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}\ge2.
\]
For every even \(n\), equality holds in the ratio bound, and the even positive integers form an infinite sequence. Thus
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
=2-\frac4n+\frac4{n^2}\longrightarrow2
\]
along the even integers, which gives the reverse inequality for the full limit inferior. Therefore that limit inferior equals \(2\).

If \(n\) is prime, its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(n\), so \(\ell(n)=n\). Substitution into the exact formulas yields
\[
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=2n,
\]
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
=2(n-1)^2+2-2n
=2(n-1)(n-2),
\]
and
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
=n\left(1-\frac2n+\frac{2}{n^2}\right)
=n-2+\frac2n.
\]
As a smallest-margin audit, at \(n=3\) the formulas give \(\ell(3)=3\), \(\Phi_3^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=6\), \(\Phi_{3,3}(4)=10\), gap \(4\), and ratio \(5/3\); these values agree directly with the sole eligible equal-square size \(k=1\) and with \(\textnormal{prop:r4-reduction}\).

proposed.statement:
For \(n_B=n_S=n\), one has \(\Phi_{n,n}(R)\ge \Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(R)\) for every \(R\). In particular, for \(R=4\) and every \(n\ge3\),
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)=2(n-1)^2+2,
\qquad
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)\le n^2,
\]
and equality in the second display holds if and only if \(n\) is even. Consequently,
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)\ge (n-2)^2>0
\]
and
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
\ge 2-\frac4n+\frac4{n^2}.
\]
Equality in the ratio bound holds if and only if \(n\) is even. Thus this lower bound tends to \(2\), the actual ratio tends to \(2\) along the even integers, and its limit inferior over all integers \(n\to\infty\) equals \(2\).
proposed.justification: The exact least-divisor formula shows that the catalog is not merely a notational enlargement of the published equal-square family: unequal covering rectangles strictly improve focal retention for every balanced size \(n\ge3\), even sizes give the sharp factor-two asymptotic lower envelope, and prime sizes give ratio \(n-2+2/n\).
proposed.gap: The published equal-square calculation optimizes only over equal block sizes and does not identify that its support-four optimum is \(2n^2/\ell(n)\), nor the resulting exact separation from the covering paired-rectangle frontier.
proposed.consumer: Researchers using the published equal-block rule can compute its exact support-four benchmark from the least nontrivial divisor of the balanced population size and quantify the precise focal-size gain from allowing unequal covering rectangles.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Wire the exact support-four least-divisor classification into the target as a load-bearing proved lemma, preserve every definition needed by the direct all-resolution equal-square construction, and remove the unused affine-frontier dependency.

proposed.comparator_claim: Theorem 3.2 establishes validity of Procedure 3.2 for any equal block size \(k\); within that published equal-square family the retained focal count is \(2nk\).
proposed.matched_by: The covering paired-rectangle frontier weakly dominates the published equal-square optimum for every resolution \(R\) by an explicit equal-square-profile construction. At \(R=4\), lem:r4-least-divisor-classification proves the exact published-subclass optimum \(\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=2n^2/\ell(n)\), where \(\ell(n)\) is the least divisor of \(n\) at least two, and compares it with the exact covering paired-rectangle frontier. Even \(n\) gives the sharp factor-two asymptotic lower envelope, while prime \(n\) gives ratio \(n-2+2/n\).

proposed.comparator_claim: The randomization test described in Procedure 1 is valid conditionally at any level.
If \(T\) is imputable, the randomization test is valid at any level \(\alpha\).
Then, \(W\) is uniformly distributed conditional on the event \(\{W\in\mathcal B\}\).
If \(T\) is effect increasing, then \(p^{L+}(D^{\mathrm{obs}},\theta)\) is non-decreasing in \(\theta\).
The concentration probability is maximized when all the \(a_i\) are \(\pm1\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: Synchronize the published-comparator entry with the preserved all-resolution dominance and the new exact support-four least-divisor, even-size, and prime-size conclusions.

prose_updates.tldr: For independently and uniformly half-randomized populations on two unequal market sides, the optimal covering rectangle at required support \(R\) reduces to a finite residual catalog depending only on \(R\). For \(R\ge4\) and \(n_B,n_S\ge4R\), the exact frontier is the maximum of finitely many affine catalog scores and every tie is retained. On balanced squares, the covering paired-rectangle frontier weakly dominates the published equal-square subclass for every resolution. At \(R=4\), if \(\ell(n)\) is the least divisor of \(n\) at least two, then the published equal-square optimum is exactly \(2n^2/\ell(n)\), while the covering optimum is \(2(n-1)^2+2\). Their exact ratio is \(\ell(n)(1-2/n+2/n^2)\): even sizes form the sharp factor-two asymptotic lower envelope, whereas prime sizes have ratio \(n-2+2/n\). A constant-incidence sampler implements the selected event, and null-adjusted focal outcomes yield exact one-sided inversion for a sharp constant total effect. No universal collapse of the catalog to diagonal unit residuals is claimed.

project_justification.gap: The closest exact two-sided-market method proves validity for selected equal blocks and treats block choice within that published equal-square subclass; it neither states the general dominance of that subclass by covering paired rectangles nor identifies the support-four optimum \(2n^2/\ell(n)\) from the least nontrivial divisor. General biclique methods establish validity and power guidance but do not classify the optimal covering paired rectangle. Marketplace bias-and-variance analyses motivate the design problem but do not solve this exact rectangle optimization, and existing one-dimensional subset-sum purification does not preserve a prescribed common buyer--seller target fiber.
project_justification.niche: Balanced independent randomization converts admissible covering rectangles into two coupled half-sum profiles. This structure permits an exact finite residual reduction and affine phase analysis for unequal market-side sizes. On balanced squares it contains every published equal-square profile, and at \(R=4\) it yields an exact arithmetic classification of that benchmark through \(\ell(n)\), the least divisor of \(n\) at least two, without asserting an unrestricted-biclique optimum.
project_justification.fill: A two-stage concentration argument bounds the residual on the smaller side and uses a support-preserving residual-copy comparison to bound the larger residual. This yields a finite catalog and an exact affine frontier with all catalog ties. A direct equal-square-profile construction proves dominance over the published equal-square subclass for every resolution. At \(R=4\), every proper equal-block divisor is eligible, so the published equal-square optimum is exactly \(2n^2/\ell(n)\), versus the covering paired-rectangle value \(2(n-1)^2+2\). The exact ratio \(\ell(n)(1-2/n+2/n^2)\) has its sharp factor-two asymptotic lower envelope on even sizes and equals \(n-2+2/n\) at prime sizes. The same catalog supports an implementable conditional law and exact one-sided sharp-null inversion. Whether every catalog entry can be purified to a dominating diagonal unit-residual entry remains a separate open question.

prose_updates.related_work: Liu, Shaikh, and Toulis (2026) establish the equal \(k\)-block total-effect test and motivate the support--focal-size trade-off. The covering paired-rectangle class contains their published equal-square profiles, which gives weak dominance at every resolution. At support four, the present result proves the exact published-subclass optimum \(\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=2n^2/\ell(n)\), with \(\ell(n)\) the least divisor of \(n\) at least two, and compares it with the exact covering paired-rectangle optimum \(2(n-1)^2+2\). Even sizes give the sharp factor-two asymptotic lower envelope, while prime sizes give ratio \(n-2+2/n\). Puelz, Basse, Feller, and Toulis (2022) encode imputable tests as bicliques and motivate large bicliques, but do not supply the paired-rectangle classification. Li, Zhao, Johari, and Weintraub (2021) study interference-induced bias and variance in two-sided marketplace experiments, and Johari, Li, Liskovich, and Weintraub (2022) analyze bias under two-sided platform designs; both motivate why focal retention and design choice matter, but neither is a competing exact covering-rectangle optimization result. Basse, Feller, and Toulis (2019) provide the conditioning-mechanism validity theorem used after imputability is verified. Basse, Ding, Feller, and Toulis (2024) provide the orbit-equivariance template, while unequal rectangular profiles require a separate constant-incidence count. Luo, Dasgupta, Xie, and Liu (2021) provide discrete Fisher inversion machinery, specialized here after null-adjusted dyadic imputability and crossing monotonicity are established. Singhal (2019) motivates bilinear subset-sum profiles and one-dimensional purification, but does not furnish a coupled common-fiber-preserving reduction to diagonal unit residuals. Ye et al. (2023) provide the unequal-side marketplace consumer through Platform O's independent user-view and ad randomizations.
prose_updates.interpretation: The finite-catalog result is the actionable design certificate: for fixed resolution \(R\), one enumerates \(\mathcal C_R\), evaluates the affine scores at the two market sizes, and retains every maximizer on a phase boundary. On balanced squares, this covering design class weakly dominates the published equal-square subclass at every resolution by reproducing each eligible equal-square profile. The \(R=4\) slice has a complete arithmetic comparator: letting \(\ell(n)\) be the least divisor of \(n\) at least two, the best published equal-square profile retains \(2n^2/\ell(n)\), while the optimal covering paired rectangle retains \(2(n-1)^2+2\). The exact ratio is \(\ell(n)(1-2/n+2/n^2)\). Even sizes, for which \(\ell(n)=2\), attain the sharp lower envelope \(2-4/n+4/n^2\) and establish limit inferior two; prime sizes, for which \(\ell(n)=n\), have ratio \(n-2+2/n\) and therefore a linear-scale separation. These comparisons concern the published equal-square subclass, not unrestricted bicliques. The unresolved unit-residual question concerns only whether the already finite computation admits a further universal closed-form collapse; it is not needed for catalog optimality, this exact comparison, sampling, or exact one-sided inversion.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The note proves the finite residual catalog, exact affine frontier and catalog equality cases, the constant-incidence sampler, and exact one-sided inversion under the sharp constant total-effect null. On balanced squares, it proves that covering paired rectangles weakly dominate the published equal-square subclass for every resolution. At \(R=4\), it also proves the exact published equal-square comparator formula \(2n^2/\ell(n)\), the exact gap and ratio against the covering paired-rectangle optimum, the sharp even-size factor-two asymptotic lower envelope, and the prime-size ratio \(n-2+2/n\). Universal unit-residual purification remains an explicit unresolved question and is not used by those results. The note makes no claim about weak-null validity, power or confidence-width optimality, unrestricted bicliques, minimality of the \(4R\) threshold, ordinary two-sided \(95\)-percent inversion at support \(20\), or the empirical validity of the constant-effect exposure model for Platform O.
